newsitem.title: JAPAN: Scandal-hit Sumitomo plunges into red in 1996/97.
newsitem.headline: Scandal-hit Sumitomo plunges into red in 1996/97.

text.p: Japan's Sumitomo Corp, hit by massive copper trading losses, announced on Tuesday it went into the red in the last business year for the first time since the giant trading house was founded in 1919.
The company said its parent net losses in the year to March 31 reached 148.63 billion yen ($1.31 billion) compared with the previous year's net profit of 16.28 billion yen ($144 million).
It also made a loss on a group net basis after a profit the year before.

Takashi Nomura, senior managing director of Sumitomo, told reporters: "I regret to announce that we had net losses because of copper trading losses. We're going to tighten risk control for all commodities and financial trading."
Sumitomo said last June that it lost $2.6 billion as a result of a decade of unauthorised copper trading by former star trader Yasuo Hamanaka, who was fired in June 1996.
Hamanaka, for nearly 10 years the most influential trader in the world copper market, has pleaded guilty to charges of fraud and forgery in connection with the scandal.
The trade house said its total parent sales fell to 12.71 trillion yen ($112 billion) last business year, down by 11.7 percent from the previous year.

Of the total, the metal division's sales totalled 2.68 trillion yen ($23.7 billion), down by 40.7 percent from the previous year, mainly because of a steady decline in sales of copper products since the scandal broke out.
Sumitomo said an internal inquiry into copper losses cost nearly nine billion yen ($79.6 million), including hiring legal and accounting experts.
Sumitomo said the cost includes commission fees for financial institutions which helped Sumitomo to liquidate huge long positions Hamanaka had built in the world copper market.
Meanwhile, most other top trading houses in Japan turned in a good earnings performance for 1996/97, with Mitsubishi Corp and Itochu Corp enjoying a spurt in parent earnings.
However, Mitsubishi said Japan Leisure Card System Co, an affiliate which issues prepaid cards for "pachinko" pinball machines, made a heavy loss as a result of forged prepaid cards.
